abstract: The isotopic signatures of dissolved inorganic carbon ({delta}13C-DIC) can provide a sensitive tracer of biological and biogeochemical processes in aquatic environments. However, isotopic measurements remain uncommon within routine coastal monitoring programmes. This pilot study investigated spatial variability in {delta}13C-DIC in surface waters across twelve Northern Ireland coastal monitoring stations sampled during July 2020. We tested the relationships between {delta}13C-DIC, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) concentration, nutrients, chlorophyll-a, temperature and salinity. {delta}13C-DIC exhibited substantial spatial variability, ranging from 1.25 to 2.53{per thousand}. Significant positive relationships were observed between {delta}13C-DIC and temperature (R2 = 0.55, p = 0.009), chlorophyll-a concentration (R2 = 0.38, p = 0.045) and DIC concentration (R2 = 0.52, p = 0.012), while significant negative relationships occurred with dissolved inorganic nitrogen (R2 = 0.53, p = 0.011) and phosphate (R2 = 0.44, p = 0.026). No relationships were detected between {delta}13C-DIC and salinity, suggesting that conservative mixing processes exerted little influence on isotopic variability across the study area. Bulk DIC concentration exhibited comparatively weak associations with environmental variables. The relationships we observed indicate that biological carbon fixation and nutrient use were important controls on spatial variation in {delta}13C-DIC in the coastal waters of Northern Ireland. These findings demonstrate the potential value of {delta}13C-DIC measurements as sensitive indicators of coastal carbon-cycle dynamics and support their inclusion within future coastal monitoring and assessment programmes.
